key_insight: LLM judges detect unsafe clinical actions more reliably when given EHR evidence; apparent task completion alone is not a dependable safety signal.
clinical_relevance: Evaluating EHR-connected AI agents should assess their underlying actions and clinical evidence, not just their final answers.
method: Injected eight categories of clinical errors into verified MedAgentBench trajectories.
Compared 416 faulty trajectories with correct counterparts using six open-weight LLM judges.
Tested different evidence inputs and combined LLM judgments with an EHR-informed rule-based checker.
evidence_signal: Final-answer-only judges flagged 56% of correct trajectories, while full-trajectory evaluation reached a discrimination score of 0.75 and combined LLM–rule-based checking detected 97% of injected faults.
watch_item: These controlled benchmark results do not establish real-world clinical safety; added agent reasoning did not improve overall detection, and incorrectly reported clinical values remained hardest to detect.
paper_title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
